prompt: February 2025 was up 24.5% on February 2024, and March only 14.0%. What explains most of the gap?

choices.text: A marketing campaign in February 2025
choices.why: Nothing in the data needs one; the holiday explains it.

choices.text: Carnival moved from February to March
choices.why: Right. Each month was compared with a month that differed by a Carnival.

choices.text: February 2024 had an extra day, since it was a leap year, so its total is inflated
choices.why: An extra day in 2024 would make 2025 look worse, not better.

choices.text: Growth slowed in March
choices.why: The two months together grew 18.8%, between the two.

prompt: Which comparison gives the honest year-on-year growth for February and March?

choices.text: Both months together, against both of 2024
choices.why: Right. Both periods contain one Carnival.

choices.text: February alone, since it is the month the director asked about
choices.why: February 2024 had Carnival and February 2025 did not.

choices.text: March alone
choices.why: March 2025 had Carnival and March 2024 did not.

choices.text: The average of the two monthly percentages
choices.why: Averaging two distorted figures is not the same as comparing like periods.

prompt: What is an exogenous series, in statsmodels' exog?

choices.text: The residuals the model leaves behind once it has been fitted
choices.why: Residuals come out of a model; exog goes in.

choices.text: The test weeks, kept aside until the forecast is checked
choices.why: Those are kept away from the model, not given to it.

choices.text: A second seasonal period
choices.why: A season comes from the series itself.

choices.text: An outside series handed to the model
choices.why: Right. Here, Carnival days per week.

prompt: An analyst wants to add next month's rainfall as a regressor to improve the order forecast. What is the problem?

choices.text: Rain has no effect on orders
choices.why: It may well have one; that is not the problem.

choices.text: exog only accepts holidays
choices.why: It accepts any series.

choices.text: Its future values are unknown when forecasting
choices.why: Right. A regressor's future values must be known at forecast time.

choices.text: Rainfall is measured in millimetres and orders in units
choices.why: Units do not matter to a regression coefficient.

prompt: Adding Carnival days lowered the 26-week MAE from 362.0 to 301.3. By how many orders did it fall?
Run on the whole series, STL's October-to-December seasonal index fell from 1.023 in 2023 to 0.880 in 2025. What really happened?

choices.text: Autumn became a quieter season for meal kits
choices.why: That is STL's reading, and it is the mistake.

choices.text: The season absorbed a price rise
choices.why: Right. A smoother allowed to drift bent the season to fit a step.

choices.text: STL has a bug with multiplicative series, so its seasonal index drifts down every year
choices.why: The log made it additive; the drift has a cause in the business.

choices.text: The data for 2025 is incomplete
choices.why: Only the last three days are; months of drift need another cause.

choices.text: 0 before an event, 1 after it
choices.why: Right. Its coefficient is the size of the step.

choices.text: A moving average with a step-shaped window
choices.why: It is a column given to a model, not a smoother.

choices.text: The difference between each week and the next
choices.why: That is differencing, the I in ARIMA.

choices.text: A dummy that is 1 on holidays
choices.why: That is the Carnival column; a step stays at 1 from the event on.

prompt: panela.py multiplies the level by 0.86 after the price rise. What fall is that, in per cent?
Why could no method tell, from the data alone, whether the autumn of 2025 was a new season or a new level?

choices.text: Weekly data is too coarse
choices.why: Daily data would show the same step at the same point.

choices.text: Three years are too few for any model to estimate a season
choices.why: Three years estimate the season fine; the issue is one autumn of the change.

choices.text: STL is the wrong method for business data
choices.why: Any method faces the same ambiguity.

choices.text: Both stories fit one autumn equally well
choices.why: Right. Only knowing about the price rise separates them.

prompt: Which of these are sound responses to a regime change? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: Record its date and cause where every forecast reads them
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Model it with a step regressor
choices.why: Right, when the step is clean.

choices.text: Train only on the data after it, once there is enough
choices.why: Right, at the cost of history.

choices.text: Let a flexible smoother absorb it
choices.why: That bends trend or season and makes them wrong on both sides.

prompt: On the dashboard, 31 December showed 324 orders; the final count was 559. What share had arrived, in per cent, to the nearest whole number?
The dashboard says the last seven days were 8.9% below last year; the final data says 2.5%. Where does the difference come from?

choices.text: Christmas fell on a different weekday, which moved orders out of that seven-day window
choices.why: That changes both figures alike; only the dashboard's last days differ.

choices.text: A data error in 2024
choices.why: 2024 is complete in both comparisons.

choices.text: The last three days were still being counted
choices.why: Right. Orders are counted when paid, and payments arrive late.

choices.text: The price rise
choices.why: It affects the final data too.

prompt: On 20 May a report compares 'May so far' with 'all of April' and shows a fall. What should it compare instead?

choices.text: May so far with all of May last year
choices.why: Still a partial period against a complete one.

choices.text: The first 20 days of May with the first 20 days of April
choices.why: Right. The same number of days, counted the same way.

choices.text: Nothing: wait until June
choices.why: Waiting is an option, but a like-for-like comparison is possible now.

choices.text: May so far, doubled
choices.why: Twenty days are not half of May, and scaling ignores the weekly pattern.

prompt: How do you find out how many days it takes before a day of your data is complete?

choices.text: Compare saved snapshots with the final data
choices.why: Right. That is what snapshot.py does.

choices.text: Ask the vendor; the documentation will say
choices.why: Useful, and it should be checked against the data itself.

choices.text: Assume one day, since most systems update overnight
choices.why: Panela's took three days, and another source may take thirty.

choices.text: Look at the residuals of a decomposition
choices.why: A late-arriving day looks like a real dip there; it does not reveal the delay.

prompt: Put the checklist's four groups of questions in the order the lesson gives them.
In March, the finance team starts counting cancelled orders as negative orders. To a forecast, what does that look like?

choices.text: A new holiday
choices.why: It does not come and go; it lasts.

choices.text: Noise, which the model will average away
choices.why: A lasting drop is not noise.

choices.text: Incomplete data at the end of the series
choices.why: It affects every day from March on, not only the last few.

choices.text: A regime change
choices.why: Right. A change in counting looks exactly like a change in the business.

prompt: Match each pitfall to its symptom in Panela's data.

pairs.right: an autumn season that seems to get quieter every year
a last day at 58 per cent of its final count

right_distractors: a weekly ripple in the residuals

prompt: statsmodels takes outside series, such as Carnival days per week, through its ___ argument.
A new analyst's forecast shows Panela's orders falling 9% in the last week of December. What should be checked first?

choices.text: Whether ARIMA would have done better than the model the analyst chose for this series
choices.why: A different model fitted on incomplete data inherits the same fall.

choices.text: Whether Carnival moved
choices.why: Carnival is in February or March.

choices.text: Whether the last days are fully counted
choices.why: Right. It is the cheapest check and the commonest cause.

choices.text: Whether prices rose
choices.why: Possible, and the incomplete days are a likelier and cheaper first check.
